newsitem.title: USA: Republican leaders see Gingrich win.
newsitem.headline: Republican leaders see Gingrich win.

text.p: Republican leaders expressed confidence Sunday that House Speaker Newt Gingrich will win re-election Tuesday despite his admission he broke House ethics rules.
But the lone Republican who has publicly stated he will not vote for Gingrich said he has detected a wavering in support for the speaker who admitted to ethics violations Dec. 21.
"I still believe it's a a 50-50 proposition," said Representative Michael Forbes of New York.

"I have talked to a host of Republicans who have reached out to me over the last week and they are equally troubled," he said on NBC's "Meet the Press' programme. "I have been told by a handful of Republicans that they are leaning there very strongly" towards toppling Gingrich.
"If this were a secret ballot, I believe in my heart that unfortunately for Newt he would not be the speaker, but we would put these troubles behind us," Forbes said.

But balloting is not secret. Some time after noon Tuesday when the new Congress convenes, the 227 Republicans and 207 Democrats, with one independent who routinely votes with the Democrats, will be asked by name to elect the next speaker.
This means that if 20 Republicans abstain, Democrat leader Richard Gephardt could be elected
"It looks clear to me now that we will re-elect Newt," John Boehner, an Ohio congressman who is chairman of the Republican Conference, said on "Meet the Press."
"Newt has admitted that he has made some mistakes," he said, but added "they are not serious enough to deny him as speaker of the House."
One fellow Republican House member said Gingrich had told him Friday that he would not rule out taking himself out of contention for re-election.

"That's right," Representative Matt Salmon of Arizona said on the ABC programme "This Week" in reply to a question about his description of a telephone conversation he had with Gingrich Friday about the possibility of stepping aside. "He said he was keeping his options open and that still might be a possibility."
On Monday, Gingrich is to address a meeting of House Republicans to seek their support for re-election as speaker, the third-highest constitutional officer in the land.

Salmon said that if Republicans still are troubled after Gingrich's address, they could elect another speaker to serve while "we could get this resolved among ourselves," and then another election could be held with Gingrich up for the speaker's post.

Still, House Republican Leader Dick Armey of Texas, who was next in line to Gingrich, agreed that Gingrich would win re-election, saying on the "Fox News Sunday" programme that Forbes' comment about the vote was baseless.

"Here you have speculation," he said. "I've talked to a lot of members (of Congress), and there are an awful lot of other members who have been checked on. That's the kind of projection that I think has no foundation."

Boehner rejected arguments that Gingrich's problems would wound the Republican political agenda. "I think this next Congress will be just as productive," as the last Congress which he said was the most productive in 30 years.

Gingrich agreed "with great sadness" with a House ethics subcommittee's finding that tax-exempt funds helped to finance a partisan lecture series he conducted -- legally, the charge is that he failed to prevent this -- and that he then gave investigators misleading information on that matter.

Gingrich earned the enmity of many Democrats for his dogged pursuit of Democratic Speaker Jim Wright on ethics violations in 1989. Wright, accused of numerous violations, became the first speaker to resign before any punishment was imposed.
